title.text: Words as numbers: bag of words, TF-IDF, embeddings and distance

objects.text: How can a computer find the right clause or policy when I describe it in plain words?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 4 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Last time you learned to measure a model. Today a more basic question: how does a computer read words at all?

Computers only handle numbers, so every piece of text has to become numbers first. You will see three ways of doing that, from a simple tally to the embeddings behind search by meaning, and you will measure how close two of them are by hand.

slides.notes: By the end of today you will see how a message becomes numbers: first as word counts, then as rare-word weights, then as embeddings. You will work out four distances by hand with a pencil. And you leave with a distance cheat sheet. You will also decide where search by meaning could help or hurt in your own work.

title.text:
Your two hours: from word counts to a
search that understands a description

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_9c0d87c9.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: The search results are recorded in advance. You can ask me to run any description of yours live.

slides.notes:
We start with the simplest way to turn words into numbers, counting them, and see why it falls short. Then I show you embeddings and the four ways of measuring how close two of them are. I run a live search where a plain description finds the formal clause, term or policy, on three kinds of text.

After the break you work four distances out by hand on paper. We finish with where this helps or hurts in your own work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why can accuracy mislead when the thing you look for is rare?
2.  What do precision and recall each ask?
3.  What happens when you lower the threshold?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png
objects.alt: Three questions

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 3. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why can accuracy mislead when the thing you look for is rare? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A model that says no every time scores very high and catches nothing. In our run, always saying on time scored 90.8 percent. Ask for the baseline, precision and recall.

Question two. What do precision and recall each ask? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Precision: of the cases flagged, how many were real. Recall: of the real cases, how many were flagged.

Question three. What happens when you lower the threshold? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. The model flags more cases. It catches more real ones and also raises more false alarms.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Bag of words. A message turned into a tally of how often each word appears. The order is lost.

TF-IDF. A tally in which rare words count for more than common ones.

Embedding. A list of numbers that places a piece of text on a map of meaning.

Vector. Any list of numbers. Drawn as an arrow from the starting point.

Cosine similarity. How close the direction of two arrows is. 1 means the same way.

title.text:
A bag of words turns a
message into a row of counts

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_bow_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A bag of words turns a message into a row of counts

objects.text: Like a tally sheet at the till: one mark each time a word appears.

runs.text: Message B has "the" twice and "late" once.
The order is lost: "man bites dog" and "dog bites man" give the same counts.
Real term: bag of words.

slides.notes:
The simplest way to turn a message into numbers is to count words. Think of a tally sheet at a shop till, one mark every time an item is sold. Here are four short invented customer messages. For each one we count how often a few words appear.

Message B has the word the twice and the word late once. Each message becomes a row of numbers. This is called a bag of words, because the words are shaken into a bag and the order is lost. Man bites dog and dog bites man give the same counts.

It is crude, and it is still useful for sorting and searching.

title.text:
TF-IDF gives rare words more weight,
because a rare word points to its message

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_tfidf_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: TF-IDF gives rare words more weight, because a rare word points to its message

objects.text: A clerk in a records room finds a file by "jerrycan". The word "the" finds nothing.

runs.text: By hand: count × (40 ÷ messages with the word).
Simplified: the real formula uses a logarithm (last column).

slides.notes:
Counting treats every word alike, but the word the tells you nothing and the word jerrycan tells you a lot. TF-IDF fixes that. Take the forty invented customer messages from our case company. For a word in message six, multiply its count by forty divided by the number of messages that contain it.

Invoice appears twice and is in four messages: two times ten is twenty. The appears once and is in twenty-two messages: one times one point eight. The rare word wins. That is a simplified version. The real formula uses a logarithm, and the last column shows the real result. The name stands for term frequency times inverse document frequency.

title.text:
An embedding places a text on a map,
and nearby places mean nearby things

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_plane_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: An embedding places a text on a map, and nearby places mean nearby things

objects.text: Two numbers place a point on a map. Give each word two numbers and it gets a place too.

runs.text: invoice (4, 1) is mostly about money.
lorry (1, 4) is mostly about trucks.
A list of numbers is a vector: draw it as an arrow.

slides.notes:
Counting cannot see meaning. The words flood and force majeure share no words, yet they are close in meaning. Here is the fix. You already know that two numbers place a town on a map, a latitude and a longitude, and that nearby towns have nearby numbers. Do the same for words.

Give each word two numbers, how much it is about money, and how much it is about trucks. Invoice and receipt point to the right. Lorry and truck point upwards. A list of numbers is called a vector, and we draw it as an arrow. Close arrows mean close meaning.

Real embeddings use hundreds of numbers, not two, but the idea is the same.

title.text:
A real embedding has 384 numbers:
nobody reads them, we compare them

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_numbers_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A real embedding has 384 numbers: nobody reads them, we compare them

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026, model all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Gold: close in meaning.

slides.notes:
This is a real embedding, from a recorded run. I used a small open model called all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Its model card says it turns a sentence into a vector of three hundred and eighty-four numbers, and that it was trained on more than a billion pairs of related sentences.

Here are the first eight numbers for three texts. The first is a plain question about heavy rain flooding the road. The second is the force majeure clause, which is about events beyond anyone control. The third is the governing law clause. No person can read these numbers.

We only compare them. The question and the force majeure clause score zero point three six against each other. The governing law clause scores zero point zero three.

title.text:
Straight-line distance asks how
far apart two arrow tips are

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_euclid_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Straight-line distance asks how far apart two arrow tips are

objects.text: A crow flying from Jinja to Mbale takes the straight line.

runs.text: From a (3, 4) to b (6, 8): 3 across, 4 up.
The straight line is 5.
Real term: Euclidean distance. Smaller is closer.

slides.notes:
Now the four ways of measuring how close two arrows are. First, the straight line. A crow flying from Jinja to Mbale does not follow the road. It flies straight. Take two arrow tips, a at three, four, and b at six, eight. From a to b you go three across and four up.

Draw that on squared paper and the straight line between them measures exactly five. That is the three, four, five triangle. Mathematicians call it Euclidean distance, after the Greek geometer, and it is what a ruler measures. Smaller is closer. Zero would mean the two tips sit on the same spot.

title.text:
City-block distance adds the
walk across to the walk up

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_manhattan_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: City-block distance adds the walk across to the walk up

objects.text: A boda boda rider in town must follow the streets, block by block.

runs.text: From a to b: 3 across + 4 up = 7 blocks.
The straight line is 5, but the streets make it 7.
Real term: Manhattan distance. Smaller is closer.

slides.notes:
Second, the city block. A boda boda rider in town cannot cut through buildings. The rider goes along one street and then up another. From a to b that is three blocks across and four blocks up, seven in all. The straight line was five, but the streets make it seven.

Mathematicians call this the Manhattan distance, after the street grid of that city. You only add: three plus four. Smaller is closer. It adds up every difference between the two lists of numbers.

title.text:
The dot product is an agreement score:
multiply matching numbers, then add

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_dot_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The dot product is an agreement score: multiply matching numbers, then add

objects.text: Compare a shopper's list with a shop's stock: multiply the amount wanted by the amount held, item by item, then add.

runs.text: Bigger is closer. Long arrows score higher.

slides.notes:
Third, the agreement score. Picture a shopper with a list and a shop with its stock. For each item, multiply the amount wanted by the amount in stock, then add everything up. A big total means the list and the stock agree. Do it with arrows. For a with b: three times six is eighteen, four times eight is thirty-two, and the total is fifty.

For a with c: three times four is twelve, four times three is twelve, total twenty-four. The real name is the dot product. Bigger means closer. Notice that b is a long arrow, and long arrows pick up bigger scores just for being long.

title.text:
Cosine compares only the
angle between two arrows

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_cosine_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Cosine compares only the angle between two arrows

objects.text: Two cyclists on the same road: one rides twice as far, and both face the same way.

runs.text: a and b: no angle. Cosine 1.00.
Real term: cosine similarity. 1 same way, 0 unrelated.

slides.notes:
Fourth, the angle. Picture two cyclists on the same road. One rides twice as far as the other, but both face the same way. Their direction is identical. The arrows a and b are like that: b is twice as long, and there is no angle between them, so the cosine is one.

Arrow c points a little differently, sixteen degrees away. Its cosine is twenty-four divided by five times five, which is zero point nine six. The real name is cosine similarity. One means the same direction, zero means unrelated, at a right angle. Cosine ignores length, and for text that is usually what we want, because a long passage should not win just for being long.

title.text:
The four measures can pick different
winners, so know which one you use

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_compare4_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The four measures can pick different winners, so know which one you use

objects.text: Which is closer to a: the long arrow b or the short arrow c?

runs.text: Straight line and city blocks pick c.
Agreement score and cosine pick b.
Cosine is widely used for text, because length says little about meaning.

slides.notes:
Now put all four on one question. Which is closer to a: the long arrow b, or the short arrow c?

The straight line says c, one point four against five. City blocks say c, two against seven. The agreement score says b, fifty against twenty-four, because b is long. Cosine says b, one against zero point nine six, because b points exactly the same way. They disagree, and none of them is wrong.

They measure different things. For text, cosine is widely used, because the length of a passage tells you little about its meaning. When a vendor says similarity, ask which measure.

title.text:
Demonstration: describe a clause in
plain words and find its formal name

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_ff7e641d.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: describe a clause in plain words and find its formal name

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: The right term in the top three.
A word search that finds nothing.
Compare scores only within one search.

slides.notes:
Now the live demonstration. I type a plain description, and the computer returns the formal clause, term or paragraph that matches. Four steps. I describe it in plain words. The model turns my description into three hundred and eighty-four numbers. It compares those numbers with the numbers of ten passages, using cosine.

And it ranks them, showing the top three. Next to it I show a plain word search, which looks only for shared words. You choose the kind of text: contract clauses, finance terms or HR policy paragraphs. Watch for the right answer in the top three, and watch for the word search finding nothing at all.

title.text:
Contract clauses: the right clause came
first for all four plain descriptions

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_fb6098b1.png
objects.alt: Contract clauses: the right clause came first for all four plain descriptions

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026. Gold: the right clause. Scores: cosine.

slides.notes:
Here are the recorded results for contract clauses. On the left, four descriptions in plain words. What happens if heavy rain floods the road and the delivery cannot get through?

The model puts force majeure first, at zero point three six. Who pays us back if the supplier mistake costs us money?

Indemnity, first. Can we walk away without giving a reason?

Termination for convenience. The contract keeps running every year unless we say something in time?

Automatic renewal. In the last column, a plain word search finds the right clause for three of the four, and for the flood question no clause shares a single word with the description.

title.text:
Finance terms: first once, in the top three
for three of four, so a person still chooses

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_a24ea585.png
objects.alt: Finance terms: first once, in the top three for three of four, so a person still chooses

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026. The right term was fourth for the second description.

slides.notes:
The same run on finance and invoice terms. This one is messier, and I show it on purpose. For the money we owe the maize miller, the right term, accounts payable, came second behind depreciation. For three-way match, the right term came first. For make sure our books match what the bank says, bank reconciliation came second, behind bad debt write-off.

And for the shop that sent back damaged bags, the right term, credit note, came fourth, behind accounts receivable. That is a reasonable answer to the question, because the shop does owe us money. Search by meaning gives a shortlist, and a person picks from it.

title.text:
HR policy: the right paragraph was in the top
three for all four, and word search found none first

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_36806265.png
objects.alt: HR policy: the right paragraph was in the top three for all four, and word search found none first

objects.text: All 12 searches: right answer first 7, in the top three 11; word search first 4.

slides.notes:
And HR policy paragraphs. The person afraid to report a colleague who steals stock gets whistleblowing, first. The malaria message gets sick leave, first. The unhappy employee who wants to complain gets the disciplinary procedure first and the grievance procedure second. The person who wants to quit gets the notice paragraph second.

In all four the right paragraph is in the top three, and the word search never puts the right one first. Over all twelve searches: meaning search had the right answer first in seven and in the top three in eleven. Word search had it first in four.

title.text:
Four measures agree when arrows have
equal length, and part ways when they do not

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_agree_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Four measures agree when arrows have equal length, and part ways when they do not

objects.text: This model sets every arrow to length 1 as a last step. Skip it and the measures split.

runs.text: Same question, lengths left alone: straight line says bank reconciliation.
Agreement score and cosine say bad debt write-off.
No measure is right every time.

slides.notes:
Now the four measures on the real vectors. By default this model makes every arrow exactly length one as its last step. With equal lengths, straight line, agreement score and cosine always give the same order, and city blocks usually. In our twelve searches all four agreed on the top answer in eleven.

I can skip that last step and leave the lengths alone. Then they split. For the question about matching our books to the bank, the two candidate arrows have lengths four point five and five point three. The straight line and city blocks pick bank reconciliation, the right one.

The agreement score and cosine pick bad debt write-off. Check the top three, whichever measure you use.

title.text:
A 2D map of the embeddings shows the clusters,
but keeps only 18 percent of the information

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_map_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A 2D map of the embeddings shows the clusters, but keeps only 18 percent of the information

objects.text: Squash 384 numbers down to 2 and similar texts still sit together.

runs.text: Three clusters: contracts, finance, HR.
A description can sit far from its answer on the map.
The recipe is called PCA. Another is t-SNE.

slides.notes:
Can we see all this?

Not in three hundred and eighty-four directions, so we squash it into two. This is a real map of the thirty passages and twelve descriptions from today. A recipe called PCA keeps the two directions in which the points differ most. Contract clauses cluster at the top, finance terms on the right, HR paragraphs on the left.

Price adjustment, a contract clause, sits near the finance terms, which makes sense. But look at what the map loses. It keeps only eighteen percent of the variation in the numbers, a rough measure of the information. A description can sit far from its answer on the map, even though in the full numbers it is close. Use a map to see clusters, never to measure distances.

title.text:
Work out four distances by
hand for three toy arrows

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Fill in the table for the three pairs.

runs.text: Mark A, B and C on squared paper.
Straight line: measure with a ruler.
City blocks: across plus up.
Agreement: multiply matching numbers, add.
Cosine: agreement ÷ (length × length).

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_blank_5.50x3.55.png
objects.alt: A table for three pairs of toy arrows and four distance measures, with the arrow numbers and lengths above

objects.text: You keep: The twelve answers and which pair each measure calls closest.

slides.notes:
Take fifteen minutes. On squared paper, mark three points: A at three, four, B at three, one, and C at six, zero. Draw an arrow from the origin to each. For each pair, work out four numbers. For the straight line, measure with a ruler, or count across and up.

For city blocks, add the across and the up. For the agreement score, multiply matching numbers and add. For cosine, divide the agreement score by the two lengths multiplied: A is five, B is three point one six, C is six. When you have the twelve answers, ask yourself which pair each measure calls the closest. The answers will not all agree.

title.text:
Write three plain descriptions from your
own work and predict what finds them

objects.text: 10 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Invent three searches from your own documents.

runs.text: Pick three formal terms you use: a clause, an account, a policy.
Describe each in plain words, using none of its words.
Predict: will a word search find it? Will a search by meaning?
I run one or two of them live.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_2e364b62.png
objects.alt: A small table with a formal term, a plain description and two predictions to fill in

objects.text: You keep: Three descriptions and your predictions.

slides.notes:
Now ten minutes on your own work. Pick three formal terms you use, perhaps a clause in your contracts, an account name in your ledger, or a policy heading. For each, write a plain description without using any word of the term, as if you were explaining it to a new colleague.

Then predict two things. Would a plain word search find it?

Would a search by meaning find it?

Write yes, no or unsure. In the last few minutes I run one or two of your descriptions live on a small sample of your text, so bring a few short paragraphs if you would like that.

title.text:
Keep the distance cheat sheet:
four pictures, one rule each

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_cheat_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Keep the distance cheat sheet: four pictures, one rule each

objects.text: Straight line and city blocks: smaller is closer. Agreement score and cosine: bigger is closer.

slides.notes:
Here is the take-away, the distance cheat sheet. Straight line, the Euclidean distance, is what a ruler measures, and smaller is closer. City blocks, the Manhattan distance, adds up the differences one by one, and smaller is closer. The agreement score, the dot product, multiplies and adds, bigger is closer, and long arrows score higher.

Cosine looks at the angle and ignores length, and bigger is closer. If a vendor says similarity or distance, ask which one, and whether the vectors were set to length one first. Whichever you use, read the top three, because a score only ranks.

title.text:
Where would search by meaning
help or hurt in your own work?

objects.text: Think of a pile of text you search today: contracts, invoices, policies, enquiries. Where would searching by meaning help?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.80.png
objects.alt: magnifier

objects.text: Find by idea
Clauses, policies or terms you can describe but not name.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.80.png
objects.alt: doc

objects.text: Keep exact search
Codes, numbers and names must match exactly.
Write the pile of text, the option you picked and what a wrong first answer would cost.

slides.notes:
Now your own work. Think of a pile of text you search today: contracts, invoices, policies, customer enquiries. Where would searching by meaning help?

You can find a clause or policy from a description when you cannot recall its name. You can match near copies, such as the same supplier typed three ways. You can group enquiries by topic. And in some cases you should keep exact search: an invoice number or a legal citation must match exactly, and meaning search can return something merely similar.

Choose one, and say aloud what a wrong first answer would cost you. Remember that the answer is a shortlist for a person to read.
